params.question: Which of the following best distinguishes aspiration pneumonia from aspiration pneumonitis?

answers.text: Aspiration pneumonitis involves oral anaerobic bacteria, whereas aspiration pneumonia is a sterile chemical injury

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This reverses the two conditions. Aspiration pneumonitis is the chemical injury from gastric acid; aspiration pneumonia is the bacterial infection caused by oral anaerobes.

answers.text: Aspiration pneumonia is a bacterial infection by oral anaerobes requiring antibiotics, whereas aspiration pneumonitis is a chemical injury from gastric acid that resolves without antibiotics

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Aspiration pneumonia involves bacterial infection — particularly oral anaerobes in patients with poor dental hygiene — and requires antibiotic therapy. Aspiration pneumonitis is a sterile chemical inflammation from inhaled gastric acid.

answers.text: Both conditions are treated identically with broad-spectrum antibiotics and supportive care

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Only aspiration pneumonia requires antibiotics. Aspiration pneumonitis is a chemical injury that typically resolves with supportive care alone — treating it with unnecessary antibiotics drives resistance.

answers.text: Aspiration pneumonia is caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa, while aspiration pneumonitis is caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Neither statement is correct. Aspiration pneumonia is caused primarily by oral anaerobes, not Pseudomonas. Aspiration pneumonitis is not caused by any bacterium — it is a chemical injury from gastric acid.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the key distinction: aspiration pneumonia = bacterial infection (oral anaerobes) = needs antibiotics. Aspiration pneumonitis = chemical injury (gastric acid) = supportive care only.

Exactly right. Aspiration pneumonia is a bacterial infection (oral anaerobes) needing antibiotics, while aspiration pneumonitis is a chemical injury from gastric acid that resolves without antimicrobial therapy.

params.question: A 70-year-old man presents with cough and fever for 3 days. He is confused, his respiratory rate is 34 breaths per minute, blood pressure is 80/50 mmHg, and blood urea is 10 mmol/L. What is his CURB-65 score?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Count each criterion: Confusion (1), Urea >7 mmol/L (1), Respiratory rate ≥30 (1), low Blood pressure (1), and age ≥65 (1). All five are met — the score is 5.
Check again. All five CURB-65 criteria are positive: Confusion, Urea 10 (>7), RR 34 (≥30), BP 80/50 (low), and age 70 (≥65). The correct score is 5, indicating the need for urgent ICU-level care.
Close, but re-examine each component. Confusion ✓, Urea >7 ✓, Respiratory rate ≥30 ✓, Blood pressure low ✓, age ≥65 ✓ — all five are present, giving a score of 5.
Correct. All five CURB-65 criteria are met: Confusion, Urea >7 mmol/L, Respiratory rate ≥30, low Blood pressure, and age ≥65. A score of 4 or 5 mandates urgent hospital or intensive care admission.

overallFeedback.feedback: Each CURB-65 component scores 1 point: Confusion, Urea >7 mmol/L, Respiratory rate ≥30/min, low Blood pressure, and age ≥65. A score ≥2 means hospitalisation; 4–5 means ICU-level care.
Well done. A CURB-65 score of 4–5 indicates severe pneumonia requiring urgent hospital or ICU-level care. Rapid bedside scoring is a critical step in the initial assessment.

params.question: A patient is admitted with suspected community-acquired pneumonia. Which is the correct sequence before starting empirical antibiotics?

answers.text: Start intravenous antibiotics immediately, then collect blood cultures within 6 hours

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Antibiotics before cultures is the most common sequencing error. Prior antibiotic exposure sterilises blood cultures and sputum, eliminating the target organism needed for later de-escalation.

answers.text: Obtain a chest X-ray first, start antibiotics, then send sputum the next morning

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A chest X-ray is essential but does not replace microbiological sampling. Blood cultures and sputum must be collected before the first antibiotic dose, not hours or a day later.

answers.text: Collect blood cultures from two separate sites and sputum for Gram stain, then start empirical antibiotics

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Blood cultures (two sites) and sputum collection take only 5–10 minutes and must precede the first antibiotic dose. This preserves diagnostic yield without delaying treatment.

answers.text: Collect sputum for culture, give the first antibiotic dose, then draw blood cultures from one site

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Blood cultures must be drawn from two separate sites to distinguish true bacteraemia from contamination, and both blood cultures and sputum must be collected before antibiotics. Never split sample collection around the first dose.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember: the correct sequence is always blood cultures (two separate sites) and sputum first, then start empirical antibiotics. This takes only 5–10 minutes and does not delay treatment.
Exactly. Cultures first, sputum next, antibiotics immediately after — all within minutes. This sequence preserves diagnostic yield without delaying therapy.

interactions.label: A hospitalised patient on intravenous ceftriaxone and azithromycin for community

params.question: A hospitalised patient on intravenous ceftriaxone and azithromycin for community-acquired pneumonia is improving at 72 hours. Blood culture grows Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to amoxicillin. What is the most appropriate next step?

answers.text: Continue the current intravenous regimen for the full course

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Failing to de-escalate when culture results are available is the single most preventable management error in pneumonia. Every extra day of broad-spectrum therapy increases the risk of Clostridioides difficile infection and drives antimicrobial resistance.

answers.text: De-escalate to oral amoxicillin based on culture and sensitivity results

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. At 48–72 hours, review culture results and de-escalate to the narrowest effective antibiotic. The organism is sensitive to amoxicillin and the patient is improving — switching to targeted oral therapy is the standard of care.

answers.text: Add intravenous vancomycin to broaden gram-positive coverage

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Broadening coverage is the opposite of what should happen in an improving patient with a known sensitive organism. The goal at 48–72 hours is to narrow therapy, not escalate it.

answers.text: Stop all antibiotics since the patient is clinically improving

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Clinical improvement at 72 hours is encouraging but does not justify stopping antibiotics entirely. The full course must be completed — with a narrower-spectrum oral agent guided by culture results.

overallFeedback.feedback: At 48–72 hours, always review culture results. If the organism is identified and the patient is improving, de-escalate to the narrowest effective antibiotic — this is the standard of care for responsible antimicrobial stewardship.
Well done. De-escalation at 48–72 hours based on culture sensitivity is essential to limit antimicrobial resistance and complications such as Clostridioides difficile infection.
